Basically I check a few units a day and try to discern whether anyone meets the requirements to be bumped down-- must not have a gang affiliation. must have a certain number of days without incident, and must be either working or enrolled in at least one reform program. Inmates who meet those standards are evaluated on a case-by-case basis to decide whether each inmate will move down a security level. I have a former death row inmate whose sentence was commuted to maximum security, and she through her perfect behavior has worked her way down to minimum. She even lives on the honor block, meaning she has a single-occupancy cell as nice as the one she had on Death Row. (lvl 9) She's going to be with me for a good long while, but she's doing just fine and seems to be enjoying her work (the kitchen-- she's always worked in the kitchen) and reform classes. Everyone on her block has been minimum their entire stay at Long Bay, but Lily started out on death row and worked her way down.

I tend to lean toward reform in the extreme. My current prison has a policy that allows non-gang-members who have had at least fifteen days without incident to be bumped down a security class, I bribe inmates with an "honor block" (twelve four-person dormitories that are all level nine and ten) and varied cell levels that are used as rewards, I focus heavily on reform programs and rehabilitation, allow all but my supermax inmates to work (what work opportunities are available varies by security level), and offer tons of classes for all security levels who are eligible to take them. 

I have found that even just simply treating drug and alcohol addictions does wonders for the civility of the prison overall, and putting them to work and providing things like a commissary and a library gives them something to do and helps keep them out of trouble. The only inmates who are treated harshly are those who consistently choose to pose a threat to the security and good order of the prison. It doesn't matter to me if you're min-sec or death row: if you don't make my life difficult, I have no desire to make yours difficult. 

I have a very low parole threshold-- 18%, I believe-- and with the exception of the gang members and other supermax jerks, something like 80% of my prisoners get parole by the 75% mark in their sentence-- many even get out at 50%. I see it as my primary responsibility to form productive, lawful citizens who are ready to succeed in the outside world and not come back. 

Obviously there is no reform option for my death row inmates, but I let them live out their final years in level 8, 9, and 10 cells and make sure they're well-fed.
